content: This unique system has facilitated the development and implementation of innovative diagnostic tools, assays, technologies, and platforms, such as FluNet for virological data and the Tool for Influenza Pandemic Risk Assessment (TIPRA). These tools are critical for evaluating the pandemic potential of influenza viruses. Since the 2002 WHO Global Agenda on Influenza Surveillance and Control, significant advancements have been made in epidemiological surveillance and monitoring. WHO has enhanced its guidance and tools to support national, regional, and global surveillance efforts. In 1999, WHO introduced a case definition for influenza-like illness (ILI). However, after the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, a global review was conducted to refine influenza surveillance standards. This review led to the modification of the ILI case definition and the creation of a new case definition for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI). In 2015, WHO developed a manual to estimate the disease burden associated with seasonal influenza. This manual helps countries use surveillance data to generate disease burden estimates, which inform national prevention and control strategies, as well as global and regional burden estimates. Countries regularly submit national epidemiological data through the WHO FluID platform, which contributes to understanding global trends, spread, intensity, and the impact of influenza. FluID complements other platforms, such as FluNet, which captures virological data. In 2017, WHO introduced the Pandemic Influenza Severity Assessment (PISA) tool to describe the epidemiological situation and assess the severity of influenza epidemics or pandemics. This tool supports national and global risk assessments and informs public health preparedness, response, recovery measures, and resource allocation. The Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework, adopted in 2011 after four years of negotiations, represents a landmark agreement. It unites member states, industry, civil society, and other stakeholders under the principle of equitable sharing of influenza viruses with pandemic potential and the benefits derived from them. WHO and manufacturers have established legally binding Standard Material Transfer Agreements (SMTAs) to ensure the provision of pandemic-related vaccines, antiviral drugs, and diagnostics to countries. As of 2018, these agreements have committed over 400 million doses of pandemic influenza vaccine, 10 million antiviral treatment courses, 250,000 diagnostic kits, and 25 million syringes for pandemic response. The International Health Regulations (IHR) (2005), adopted in 2005 and enforced in 2007, are an international legal framework aimed at preventing, protecting against, and controlling the international spread of diseases while minimizing unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. The IHR requires states to strengthen core public health capacities, including preparedness, surveillance, and response. By 2012, all states were expected to implement plans ensuring these capacities were functional across their territories. In 2016, WHO developed the Joint External Evaluation (JEE) tool to assess countries' capacities and identify urgent needs within their health systems. WHO launched the Five-Year Global Strategic Plan to Improve Public Health Preparedness and Response (2018–2023) to strengthen the capacity of WHO and member states to implement the IHR (2005). This plan focuses on building and maintaining core capacities, strengthening event management and compliance, and measuring progress while promoting accountability. In 2012, WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on Immunization updated recommendations for influenza vaccination in target populations, including pregnant women, healthcare workers, children aged 6–59 months, the elderly, and individuals with chronic conditions. These recommendations have helped countries prioritize key target groups based on national burden data. A new SAGE working group on influenza was established in 2017 to review scientific evidence and assess the need for revising global influenza vaccine policies. The Global Action Plan for Influenza Vaccines (GAP), launched in 2006, aimed to address global shortages and inequitable access to pandemic influenza vaccines. GAP focused on increasing seasonal vaccine use, expanding vaccine production capacity, and promoting research and development of more effective vaccines. Through GAP, influenza vaccine production technology was transferred to 14 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), significantly increasing global vaccine production capacity. WHO developed the Public Health Research Agenda for Influenza in 2009 to generate evidence for strengthening public health guidance and actions to mitigate the impact of pandemic, zoonotic, and seasonal influenza. A progress review in 2013 highlighted substantial funding and progress in global influenza research but emphasized the need for further work. In 2017, WHO updated the research agenda to address unmet public health needs and promote high-priority influenza research over the next 5–10 years. WHO collaborates with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) to promote the One Health approach, which emphasizes cross-sectoral coordination to address public health threats at the human-animal-ecosystem interface. The 2010 Tripartite Agreement set a strategic direction for these organizations to work closely together, reaffirmed in 2017 with a commitment to maintaining momentum in preventing and controlling zoonotic influenza. Following the 2013–2016 Ebola crisis, WHO launched the Health Emergencies Programme (WHE) in 2016 to address the full risk management cycle, including prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. WHE leads and coordinates international responses to disease outbreaks and provides effective relief and recovery to affected populations. The program operates with a unified structure across headquarters, regional offices, and country offices, comprising five technical and operational departments. During health emergencies, including influenza pandemics, WHE manages responses through the Incident Management System outlined in the WHO Emergency Response Framework. Influenza surveillance is fundamental to understanding the virus. Over the past decade, the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) has been strengthened, with 130 member states sharing influenza viruses with GISRS in 2017. However, some countries still lack the capacity to detect novel influenza viruses, a key component of IHR (2005) core capacities. Improvements in data and virus sharing are essential for accurate risk assessments of influenza viruses with pandemic potential. Understanding influenza morbidity, mortality, and economic burden is crucial for developing national prevention, control, and preparedness policies. Most burden estimates come from high-income countries, but additional studies in lowand middle-income countries are needed to better understand geographical and risk group-specific burdens. Regional and global collaboration can help pool data and extrapolate trends to improve understanding. To support pandemic preparedness, WHO developed guidance on risk-based strategies and approaches for pandemic influenza preparedness and response. In 2018, WHO published a checklist to help countries develop or update their plans. However, as of September 2018, many countries still lacked updated or publicly available influenza preparedness plans. Pandemic preparedness planning should align with national health security efforts, such as the Joint External Evaluation (JEE) and National Action Plans for Health Security (NAPHS), to maximize efficiency and utilize existing systems effectively. Nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as social distancing in schools, workplaces, and events, are critical tools for limiting influenza transmission and spread. During the 1918 pandemic, NPIs were the only available interventions, and historical evidence highlights their effectiveness when implemented early and in layers. Since the 2009 pandemic, many countries have integrated NPIs into their national influenza pandemic preparedness plans or published NPI guidelines.
